content:
Democratic Representative Jimmy Gomez of California announced on Monday that he will resign from Congress effective December 1, hours after the House Ethics Committee released a report finding “substantial evidence” that he engaged in sexual misconduct toward a congressional staffer. The bipartisan panel concluded that Gomez violated House rules by making unwelcome sexual advances and engaging in unwelcome sexual contact, and by disregarding the power imbalance inherent in his relationship with House staff.

The report, released on November 23, described a 2024 incident in which Gomez allegedly reached under a female staffer’s skirt and underwear at a Washington, D.C., bar, and later groped her in his office, according to [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/23/politics/house-ethics-committee-reports-jimmy-gomez). The committee said it found the former staffer, identified in the report only as “Witness 1,” to be credible, and determined that her account was consistent with the evidence it gathered. The panel also found that Gomez’s conduct caused the aide “significant and ongoing distress” and contributed to her decision to leave House employment altogether.

The committee noted that the behaviour could constitute criminal sexual assault under District of Columbia law, including misdemeanor sexual abuse, a point also reported by [NPR](https://www.kdlg.org/as-heard-on-npr/2026-11-23/california-democrat-rep-gomez-resigns-following-ethics-report-on-sexual-misconduct-allegations). It did not, however, recommend any particular sanction. The panel wrote that it decided to publish its findings in part to raise awareness of Gomez’s misconduct and to warn the wider House community, even though there is likely not enough time left in the current Congress for the chamber to pursue formal punishment, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Gomez, who is serving his fifth term and turns 52 this week, responded within an hour of the report becoming public. In a statement, he said he had “strong disagreements with the Committee’s report and its conclusions,” arguing that it omitted key portions of his testimony and selectively quoted his statements. “I also have serious concerns about the process,” he said. “In my interview, I answered the Committee’s questions only to see my statements selectively quoted, disparaged, and disregarded throughout the final report, to which I was given no opportunity to respond.”

At the same time, Gomez said he recognised the seriousness of the report and took “full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage.” He added that he saw “no other alternative than to resign, effective December 1, to allow for my staff to close out important constituent casework and needs.”

The investigation began in April 2026, after public reporting that Gomez had been seen kissing a different congressional aide at a 2023 party hosted by then-Representative Eric Swalwell, according to The Wall Street Journal. The committee formally opened its inquiry in August, after a woman accused Gomez of sexual assault and harassment through her attorneys. In the course of the probe, Gomez disclosed interactions with two women. With one of them, he described one occasion of consensual kissing and acknowledged an extramarital affair; the committee also interviewed a second woman, a House staffer, after Gomez disclosed a past consensual sexual relationship with her. The panel concluded that the interactions violated House rules regardless, because they involved unwelcome sexual advances toward staff.

The woman’s attorneys said in a statement to CNN that the panel’s report “confirms that Representative Gomez sexually harassed and assaulted our client while she was a staffer on Capitol Hill.” The report also recorded that the woman had “repeatedly referenced a toxic and predatory culture” on Capitol Hill — a point the committee echoed in its own language, writing that Gomez’s conduct “also reflects a broader environment of sexual misconduct and toxic working conditions in some Capitol Hill offices which the Committee is determined to address.”

Gomez’s resignation is the latest in a series of departures that have shaken the House this year. According to CNN, he is the third member of Congress to resign in 2026 in the face of sexual misconduct allegations, as the chamber has reckoned repeatedly with bombshell harassment claims against members of both parties. The pattern has put the House’s internal accountability system under fresh scrutiny — the same year [President Trump signed the Epstein Files Transparency Act](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/trump-signs-epstein-files-transparency-act-november-2026), another measure born of demands for transparency in Washington: the Ethics Committee, evenly split between five Democrats and five Republicans, has now published three damning reports in a single year, yet in each case the member has left office before the House could vote on any punishment.

The timing of Gomez’s departure is also politically significant. He was not set to return to Congress in January in any case, having lost his re-election bid earlier this month to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres, a democratic socialist, in his Los Angeles-area seat. His resignation on December 1 therefore brings forward by a month a departure that voters had already decided — but it also leaves his district without representation for the final weeks of the session, and raises the question of when a special election will be held to fill the seat for the next Congress, a process that will fall to California’s governor.

Gomez, the founder of the House Dads Caucus, had built a profile as a champion of family-friendly workplace policies in Congress — a record that now sits in sharp contrast to the findings against him. The committee’s report made a point of the power imbalance at the heart of the case: a member of Congress, it said, holds authority over the careers of the young staffers who work in and around the institution, and that imbalance made the conduct more serious, not less.

The report also underlines a wider problem that the Ethics Committee itself acknowledged. The House employs thousands of staffers, many of them young and early in their careers, and the committee’s warning — that it is “determined to address” a broader environment of misconduct — suggests that more scrutiny of Capitol Hill workplaces may follow. For now, though, the immediate consequence is clear: a five-term congressman will leave office on December 1, his career ended not by the voters who had already rejected him, but by an ethics report that found he had abused the trust placed in him as a member of the House. The House will now have to decide whether the committee’s warning about a toxic culture on Capitol Hill leads to concrete reforms, or whether Gomez’s resignation is simply the latest in a cycle of scandal, report and departure that repeats itself.
summary: Democratic Representative Jimmy Gomez of California will resign from Congress on December 1 after the House Ethics Committee found “substantial evidence” that he engaged in sexual misconduct toward a congressional staffer, making him the third member to quit this year over such allegations.
title: Jimmy Gomez to resign from Congress after House Ethics Committee finds sexual misconduct
